metadata.working_title: 24-year-old woman, two days of vomiting and diarrhea, brought through from triage
metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: I can't keep anything down and I feel really weak.
metadata.final_diagnosis: Mild diabetic ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes, set off by gastroenteritis and reduced insulin doses, with hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L) and mild hypomagnesemia from gastrointestinal losses. The potassium is low before any insulin is given, so insulin waits until it has been replaced.
learning_objectives: Check a glucose, a venous gas, a chemistry and ketones in a vomiting patient with diabetes, and recognize ketoacidosis when the patient looks only mildly unwell.
Grade the ketoacidosis as mild from the pH, the bicarbonate and the mental state.
Read the potassium before giving insulin. Under 3.5 mEq/L, replace potassium first and hold insulin until it is back above 3.5.
Give fluid first, and know what fluid alone does and does not fix.
Start insulin without a bolus once the potassium allows, by infusion or by subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin in mild ketoacidosis.
Plan what follows insulin: dextrose in the fluids when the glucose falls under 250 mg/dL, potassium continued, and insulin not stopped because the glucose looks better.
metadata.teaching_frame: The reflex in ketoacidosis is insulin. In about one patient in ten or twenty the potassium is already low on arrival, and insulin drives it lower. This patient looks well enough that nothing feels urgent, which is what makes the reflex easy to follow. The case lets the learner give insulin early, shows what it does, and lets them undo it.

care_setting.label: Urban academic emergency department
care_setting.detail: Adult emergency department. Point-of-care glucose and ketone testing, a step-down unit that runs insulin infusions and intravenous potassium on telemetry, and endocrinology on call by phone.

arrival.line: Walked in with her roommate and was brought through from triage to a monitored room.

patient.background:
Graduate student. Type 1 diabetes since age 11, on insulin glargine 18 units at night and insulin lispro with meals, by pen. One admission with ketoacidosis, at diagnosis. Appendix removed at 15. Takes a combined contraceptive pill. No other medical problems, no allergies. Drinks a little on weekends, no drugs.

Her roommate had vomiting and diarrhea three days ago. Two days ago she started vomiting, then had watery diarrhea. Because she was not eating she took no mealtime insulin, halved her long-acting insulin the first night and skipped it last night. Since yesterday she has been very thirsty, passing a lot of urine, and weak. Her meter read 380 this morning. She has no ketone strips at home.
patient.presenting_appearance: A slim young woman lying on the stretcher with a vomit bowl, tired and dry-lipped, breathing a little deeply. She answers clearly. Her roommate is in the chair.
patient.ems_handover_text: Twenty-four year old woman with type 1 diabetes, two days of vomiting and diarrhea after her roommate had the same. Not eating, so she cut back and then stopped her insulin. Thirsty and weak since yesterday. Rate 112, pressure 104 over 64, respirations 22, saturation 99 percent, temperature 37.3. No sugar done at triage.
patient.arrival_handover: Twenty-four year old woman, two days of vomiting and diarrhea, says she feels weak and can't keep fluids down. She looked dry and worn out so I brought her straight through.
patient.handover_authoring_note: Section 3.2. Two sentences, 31 words. No vital sign, no past history, no medication, no pertinent negative. It leaves out the diabetes on purpose: the triage nurse did not ask, and the learner finds it by asking or by checking a sugar.

phase_notes.count_justification: Five clinical phases and one terminal. Arrival, potassium replaced, treated, and the two phases of the wrong order: potassium falling after early insulin, and recovering from it. No halted phase and no arrest.
phase_notes.no_clock: Nothing happens to her because the learner waited. Every timed rule is the delayed consequence of an action, measured from the moment its guard became true. Approved by the directing physician on 6 October 2026.
phase_notes.order_is_carried_by_phases: The condition language cannot express order. Insulin given in the arrival phase leads to potassium_falling. The same insulin given in potassium_replaced leads to treated.

phases.label: Mild ketoacidosis, potassium low, nothing given
phases.clinical_description: Tired, dry, breathing a little deeply, fully alert. Glucose 348, pH 7.27, bicarbonate 16, potassium 3.1. Fluid helps her circulation and does not change the question, which is what has to happen before insulin.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia with a slightly flattened T wave and a QTc of 460, as the phase's twelve-lead report says. The monitor lead cannot draw a U wave. Model output.

transitions.narration: She says her arms and legs feel heavy and her heart is fluttering. Her rate has gone up.
transitions.debrief_note:
Insulin was given while her potassium was 3.1. Insulin moves potassium into cells, and hers fell to 2.6. She became weak and her ECG changed.

This is the decision the case is built around. In ketoacidosis the body is short of potassium even when the blood level looks normal, and vomiting and diarrhea had already taken hers low. The potassium result comes before the insulin. Under 3.5, replace it and hold insulin until it is back above 3.5.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Insulin moves potassium into cells within minutes, and the 2024 consensus report says to delay insulin when the potassium is under 3.5 mmol/L to avoid arrhythmia and respiratory muscle weakness. The size of the fall (3.1 to 2.6) and the ten seconds are teaching choices. Ten seconds stands for about an hour. Model output.

transitions.narration: That potassium has run through on the pump. Do you want a repeat level?
transitions.debrief_note:
Potassium was replaced before insulin. The repeat level is 3.6.

Twenty seconds here stands for several hours of infusion: four to six at 10 mEq an hour, less at a faster rate through a central line. This is the slow part of the real case and insulin waits for it. The wait has a cost. With no insulin on board her ketones keep rising, which is the reason to start the potassium promptly.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. A rise from 3.1 to 3.6 is taken as about 40 to 60 mEq, by a rough rule that often underestimates the need in ketoacidosis. Compressed openly, and the nurse says the infusion takes a while. Model output.

phases.label: Potassium back above 3.5, insulin not yet started
phases.clinical_description: Unchanged to look at. Potassium 3.6, glucose 320, pH 7.26, ketones a little higher. She is still in ketoacidosis, and now insulin is safe to start.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, T wave fuller than on arrival, as the phase's report says. Model output.

transitions.narration: Her sugar is coming down on the insulin, 266 on the meter, and she says the sick feeling is easing. Her rate is settling.
transitions.debrief_note:
Insulin was started with the potassium above 3.5 and potassium still running. Her glucose is falling and the ketones are clearing.

From here the work is watching. The consensus report asks for glucose every one to two hours, potassium two hours after insulin starts and every four hours after that, and a plan for when the glucose gets under 250.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Ten seconds stands for about an hour. Model output.

phases.label: On insulin with the potassium replaced
phases.clinical_description: Nausea easing, rate settling. Glucose 268, pH 7.30, bicarbonate 18, potassium 3.7. The intended endpoint. She needs dextrose in the fluids soon, and insulin until the ketones clear.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, T waves normal, as the phase's report says. Model output.

phases.label: Potassium driven down by insulin
phases.clinical_description: Weak in the arms and legs, aware of her heartbeat, still alert. Potassium 2.6. The ECG shows flat T waves, larger U waves and a longer QT. No clock leaves this phase. Holding insulin and giving intravenous potassium get her out.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia with a nearly flat T wave and a QT of about 520 ms, as the phase's report says. The report also describes U waves and occasional ventricular ectopic beats, and the monitor draws neither. Model output.

transitions.when: flag potassium_iv_given set AND flag insulin_stopped set
transitions.narration: The potassium has run through and the insulin is on hold. She says her arms feel stronger. Her rate has come back down.
transitions.debrief_note:
You held the insulin and replaced the potassium, and she recovered. Seeing that a treatment is hurting the patient and withdrawing it is a skill.

Insulin restarts once the potassium is above 3.5.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own actions. Twenty seconds stands for several hours of infusion. Model output.

phases.label: Potassium replaced after early insulin, insulin on hold
phases.clinical_description: Strength back. Potassium 3.6, glucose 285, still in ketoacidosis with insulin on hold. Restarting insulin moves her to the treated phase.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, T wave fuller again, as the phase's report says. Model output.

transitions.narration: Insulin is back on and her sugar is coming down, 266 on the meter. Her rate is settling.
transitions.debrief_note: Insulin was restarted with the potassium above 3.5. This is where the first dose belonged.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. The flag is granted by the second administration of infusion or subcutaneous insulin. Model output.

phases.authoring_note: Same numbers as potassium_replaced. Two phases because the exits differ: here the insulin flag is already set, so the exit is the second administration.

phases.clinical_description: Terminal phase entered when the learner confirms a handoff.

tag_vocabulary.note: Harmful is not used. Nothing halts this case.

flag_namespace_note: Flags are permanent. insulin_given is set by any insulin, insulin_running by an infusion or a subcutaneous dose, insulin_stopped by the hold action, and insulin_restarted by the second administration of an infusion or subcutaneous dose. A learner who gave both an infusion and a subcutaneous dose before the hold has already set insulin_restarted, which is a known gap.

prompt.text: She's not on a monitor yet. Do you want her hooked up?

case_actions.debrief_note: Nothing shows until the monitor is on. In this patient it matters for a second reason: a low potassium and the treatment for it are both reasons to watch the rhythm.
Fluid, potassium and an insulin infusion all need a line.
Useful when potassium, insulin and fluid are all running, because potassium is not mixed into every line. Not scored.

prompt.guard: phase is presentation AND NOT study fingerstick_blood_sugar ordered
prompt.text: She looks dry and she's breathing deeply. Do you want a fingerstick glucose?

case_actions.debrief_note:
A bedside glucose takes seconds and it is what turns a stomach bug into a different problem. The triage note did not mention diabetes. Any vomiting adult who looks dry or is breathing deeply gets one.

Repeated hourly once insulin is running.

The pH is one of the three things that make the diagnosis and it sets the severity. Hers is 7.27, which with a bicarbonate of 16 and a clear head is mild ketoacidosis in the 2024 consensus report. A venous sample is enough. An arterial puncture adds pain and no information here.
Accepted in place of the venous gas. An arterial sample is not needed to diagnose or follow ketoacidosis when the saturation is normal, and it hurts.

case_actions.expectation_label: Chemistry, for the potassium and the anion gap

prompt.guard: phase is presentation AND NOT study basic_chemistry_chem_7 ordered
prompt.text: Do you want labs sent? I can send a chemistry and a gas off the line.

case_actions.debrief_note:
Two numbers on this panel run the case. The anion gap of 18 with a bicarbonate of 16 is the acidosis. The potassium of 3.1 is the reason insulin waits.

Most patients in ketoacidosis arrive with a normal or high potassium, because acidosis and lack of insulin move it out of cells. The consensus report puts a level under 3.5 on arrival at 5 to 10 percent of patients. Two days of vomiting and diarrhea is how she got there.

A blood beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 mmol/L or more is the ketone criterion in the 2024 consensus report, and it is the number that says when the ketoacidosis has resolved (under 0.6). Urine ketones lag behind and can look worse as she gets better.
Ketones and glucose in the urine support the diagnosis. The reason to send it is the search for a trigger: urinary infection is one of the commonest. Hers shows none.
A woman of 24 who is vomiting gets a pregnancy test whatever she says about her pill. Pregnancy lowers the glucose at which ketoacidosis occurs and raises the stakes. Hers is negative.
Accepted in place of the urine test. Negative.

prompt.text: She says her heart is fluttering. Do you want a twelve-lead?

case_actions.debrief_note:
A potassium of 3.1 is a reason for an ECG and a monitor. At that level many tracings are normal. Hers shows subtle T wave flattening and small U waves. After insulin given too early the T waves flatten, the U waves grow and the QT lengthens.

The ECG is a rough guide to potassium. A normal tracing does not mean a normal level.

Low at 1.5. A low magnesium often travels with a low potassium after vomiting and diarrhea, and it makes the potassium harder to correct. The consensus report does not discuss magnesium. This is general teaching on hypokalemia.

Normal on arrival, as it usually is, and expected to fall with insulin. The consensus report advises against routine phosphate replacement and considers it when the level is low with muscle weakness or respiratory or cardiac compromise. The report prints the cutoff as under 1.0 mmol/L. Older guidance used 1.0 mg/dL. Check your own protocol.
A white count of 13 is common in ketoacidosis without infection. It is a stress response and does not on its own mean she needs antibiotics.
Normal. Lipase is often raised in ketoacidosis without pancreatitis, sometimes several times the upper limit, so a raised one would have needed interpreting with the abdomen.
Normal. Her acidosis is ketones.
At the top of the normal range. A high osmolality with a very high glucose and little ketosis would be the hyperosmolar state, which she does not have.
Clear. Pneumonia is a common trigger and she has no cough, so this was optional.

Her cramps fit the gastroenteritis, her abdomen is soft with no guarding and her appendix is out. A scan adds radiation and delay for a young woman.

Abdominal pain from ketoacidosis itself tracks the severity of the acidosis. In mild ketoacidosis, significant pain should not be put down to the ketoacidosis, and pain that persists as she improves is the reason to look further.

vital_effects.note: Teaching choice. Fluid is what brings her rate down. Every phase's authored rate is the rate without fluid.

prompt.text: She's dry and her pulse is fast. Do you want fluid running?

case_actions.debrief_note:
Fluid comes first. The consensus report recommends isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500 to 1000 mL an hour for the first two to four hours. Either counts here.

Watch what fluid did and did not do. Her rate came down and her glucose fell a little by dilution and by better kidney perfusion. Her bicarbonate and anion gap did not move. Fluid treats the dehydration. Insulin treats the ketoacidosis.

Fluid also dilutes the potassium slightly, which is one more reason to know the level early.
Continuing fluid after the bolus is part of treatment. Once potassium is under 5.0 the consensus report adds 20 to 30 mEq to each liter. Not scored separately from the bolus.

tag.when: phase is presentation OR phase is potassium_falling

prerequisites.failure_message: She hasn't got a line in yet. Do you want me to get IV access first?

case_actions.nurse_alert: It's on the pump and she's on the monitor. It takes a while to run in. I'll tell you when it's through.

prompt.guard: (phase is presentation AND study basic_chemistry_chem_7 resulted AND NOT flag potassium_iv_given set) OR (phase is potassium_falling AND NOT flag potassium_iv_given set)
prompt.text: I'm worried about her potassium. Do you want some running through the line?

escalation.text: Her potassium still hasn't been replaced. Do you want it running before anything else goes in?

case_actions.debrief_note:
This is the step that makes the case. Her potassium was 3.1 before any insulin. The consensus report says that when the level is under 3.5, potassium replacement begins and insulin is delayed until the level is back above 3.5, to avoid life-threatening arrhythmia and respiratory muscle weakness.

The report gives 10 mEq an hour as the starting rate. Most hospital policies allow 10 mEq an hour through a peripheral line and up to 20 with central access or a second line, with the patient on a monitor. Follow your own. Potassium is never given as a push.

The 2009 American Diabetes Association statement used 3.3 as the threshold, and many hospital protocols still do. This case uses 3.5, from the 2024 report.

The simulator compresses several hours of infusion into twenty seconds and does not model the dose.

case_actions.narration_override: She's taken the potassium and brought it straight back up.
case_actions.debrief_note: Oral potassium is a good route in a patient who can keep it down, and it is often given alongside the infusion. She is vomiting, so it did not stay in. With a level of 3.1 and insulin waiting on it, the intravenous route is the one that can be relied on. Not scored.

A low magnesium makes the kidneys waste potassium, so replacing it helps the potassium hold. It also protects against the rhythm problems of a long QT. This is standard teaching on hypokalemia and is not addressed in the consensus report.

tag.when: phase is potassium_replaced OR phase is recovering

case_actions.expectation_label: Insulin, once the potassium is above 3.5

prompt.text: The potassium has gone in. Do you want to start insulin now?

case_actions.debrief_note:
Insulin is the treatment for ketoacidosis and its timing is the lesson here.

Given once her potassium was above 3.5, it was right. Given while the potassium was 3.1, or before the result was back, it drove the level down to 2.6 and made her weak. The consensus report says to delay insulin until the potassium is above 3.5.

The report recommends a fixed-rate infusion of 0.1 units per kg per hour, and accepts subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every one to two hours for uncomplicated mild or moderate ketoacidosis. Either route counts in this case.

tag.when: phase is potassium_replaced OR phase is recovering OR phase is treated

also_satisfies.when: phase is potassium_replaced OR phase is recovering

case_actions.debrief_note:
Insulin is the treatment for ketoacidosis and its timing is the lesson here.

Given once her potassium was above 3.5, it was right. Given while the potassium was 3.1, or before the result was back, it drove the level down to 2.6 and made her weak. The consensus report says to delay insulin until the potassium is above 3.5.

The report recommends a fixed-rate infusion of 0.1 units per kg per hour, and accepts subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every one to two hours for uncomplicated mild or moderate ketoacidosis. Either route counts in this case.

Subcutaneous insulin cannot be turned off once it is in. That is one more reason to be sure of the potassium first.

An insulin bolus is not part of routine treatment. The consensus report mentions a bolus of 0.1 units per kg, intravenous or intramuscular, only when starting the infusion is going to be delayed. Some protocols differ. A bolus moves potassium into cells as fast as an infusion does, so before the potassium was replaced it carried the same risk.

case_actions.narration_override: Insulin is on hold until you say.

prompt.guard: phase is potassium_falling AND NOT flag insulin_stopped set
prompt.text: She's got weaker since the insulin. Do you want it held?

case_actions.debrief_note:
With the potassium at 2.6 and falling, holding insulin is the first step of the rescue. It goes back on once the potassium is above 3.5.

Stopping insulin in a patient who is responding is the opposite mistake. A glucose that looks better is not the end point. Resolution in the consensus report is ketones under 0.6 mmol/L with a pH of 7.3 or a bicarbonate of 18 or more, and many hospitals also use a closed anion gap. Insulin continues with dextrose until then. Basal insulin is started one to two hours before an infusion is stopped.

case_actions.narration_override: That's her long-acting insulin in, her usual dose.
case_actions.debrief_note:
She skipped her basal insulin, and that is why she is here. Giving it back is part of the treatment. The consensus report says a regimen the patient was already on 'can be continued at the usual dose', and that basal insulin 'should be started 1-2 h before cessation of intravenous insulin'.

How early to give it is not settled. The report says giving basal insulin during the infusion 'is advocated by many clinicians but avoided by others because of the risk of hypoglycaemia or hypokalaemia', and that several studies of a low dose found a shorter time to resolution and less rebound hyperglycemia.

This case counts it once insulin is running and the potassium is above 3.5, and does not score it before then. Glargine acts over hours, so the simulator does not let it drop the potassium the way rapid insulin does. That is a simplification. It also does not replace the infusion or the rapid-acting doses. Basal insulin alone will not clear the ketones.

case_actions.expectation_label: Dextrose-containing fluid, ordered for when the glucose is under 250
case_actions.narration_override: I'll have the dextrose fluid ready and switch to it when her sugar is under 250.
case_actions.debrief_note:
Once the glucose is under 250 mg/dL the consensus report changes the fluid to one containing 5 to 10 percent dextrose, so that insulin can continue until the ketones clear without the glucose going low. Ordering it ahead is the plan the receiving team needs.

Before insulin is running it does nothing useful.
Accepted as the dextrose plan once insulin is running. An infusion is the usual form.
Concentrated dextrose is for a low glucose. Hers was never under 250. It raises the glucose and the osmolality in a patient being treated for both.

Bicarbonate is not a treatment for mild ketoacidosis. The consensus report considers it only when the pH is under 7.0. Hers is 7.27, and insulin clears the acid by stopping ketone production.

It can also lower the potassium. A repeat chemistry after it shows hers slightly lower than before.

Treating her vomiting is kind and reasonable. Ondansetron lengthens the QT interval by a few milliseconds at usual doses, which matters only when the QT is already long. A low potassium and a low magnesium lengthen it too, and the drug label says to correct both first. In her, look at the ECG and start the replacement. A repeat ECG after it shows the QT about 5 ms longer, which is within measurement error. Not scored.
A reasonable antiemetic. Not scored.

The endocrinologist asks for the potassium and the gas before anything else, and gives the same order of treatment the case rewards. Calling is good practice and is what you would do before admission anyway.

Mild ketoacidosis in an alert patient does not usually need intensive care. The consensus report suggests a regular or observation unit for mild ketoacidosis and step-down for moderate. Some hospitals require intensive care for any insulin infusion.
Completion of the case. Scored on level of care and diagnoses.
Her airway is her own throughout.
Deep, slightly fast breathing with clear lungs is the body blowing off acid. In a vomiting patient it is easy to read as anxiety.
A fast pulse and slow capillary refill are the fluid she has lost.
A dry mouth and a fruity smell on the breath. Not everyone can smell ketones, so its absence means nothing.
Flat neck veins fit dehydration. No stiffness.
Fast and regular with no murmur. After early insulin, extra beats.
Clear. No pneumonia as a trigger.
Mild diffuse tenderness without guarding is common in ketoacidosis and improves with treatment. A rigid or localized abdomen would need its own explanation.
No flank or suprapubic tenderness. One point against a urinary source.
Nothing to find.
No calf swelling.
Dry with reduced turgor. Her injection sites are clean. An infected site or a foot wound is a trigger worth looking for in any patient with diabetes.
Fully alert, which is part of what makes this mild. After early insulin she has proximal weakness and reduced reflexes, which is the low potassium.
Tired and cooperative.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: The potassium has been through for a bit. Do you want a repeat level?
follow_ups.debrief_note:
Insulin waits for a number, not for a dose. The level is repeated after replacement and insulin starts when it is above 3.5. After that the consensus report checks potassium two hours after insulin starts and every four hours while it runs.

A sample sent before the infusion had run in shows the old level.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: Her sugar is coming down. What do you want in her fluids when it gets under 250?
follow_ups.debrief_note: Her glucose will reach 250 well before her ketones clear. The plan is dextrose in the fluids at that point, with insulin continued. Stopping insulin because the glucose looks normal lets the ketoacidosis return.

prompt_cap_recommendation.rationale: Five. On arrival: the monitor at 20 seconds, a bedside glucose at 40, bloods at 75, fluid at 100 and potassium at 130 once the chemistry is back. No deterioration depends on any of them, so the cap protects nothing here and five lets the potassium prompt be heard.

consultants.authoring_note: Section 11.5. The endocrinologist's advice depends on the chemistry, so there is a pending tier for the chemistry alone. Rules are ordered by phase, then by study state.

consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinologist: Hold the insulin now. Her potassium was low before it went in and insulin has pushed it lower. Give intravenous potassium on the monitor, give magnesium, get a twelve-lead, and repeat the level. Insulin goes back on when the potassium is above 3.5.

consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinologist: Good, and I'm glad the glargine is back in. Glucose every hour, potassium again in two hours and then every four, and keep potassium in the fluids. When the glucose is under 250 change to fluid with dextrose and keep the insulin going. Don't stop insulin because the sugar looks better.

Endocrinologist: Good. Glucose every hour, potassium again in two hours and then every four, and keep potassium in the fluids. When the glucose is under 250 change to fluid with dextrose and keep the insulin going. Don't stop insulin because the sugar looks better. Give her usual long-acting insulin tonight, and well before any infusion comes off.

consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinologist: If the repeat potassium is above 3.5, start insulin now. An infusion at 0.1 units per kilo an hour, or subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin, since it's mild. No bolus. Keep potassium going in the fluids.

Fluids, and intravenous potassium on a monitor, 10 an hour through a peripheral line or whatever your protocol allows. Check a magnesium. Repeat the potassium, and start insulin when it's above 3.5. correct_disposition.label: Step-down or intermediate care with telemetry
correct_disposition.explanation:
She needs hourly glucose checks, an insulin regimen that is being adjusted, intravenous potassium and a monitor. A step-down or intermediate unit does all of that.

The grade of ketoacidosis is not what puts her there. The 2024 consensus report suggests a regular or observation unit for mild ketoacidosis, and says the level of care is a clinical decision. Her potassium of 3.1 and the intravenous replacement on a monitor are what make step-down the better fit.

What the receiving team needs: the potassium before and after replacement, when insulin started and by which route, the plan for dextrose when the glucose is under 250, and that she reduced and then stopped her own insulin because she was not eating. She needs her long-acting insulin restarted, and sick-day teaching before she goes home: basal insulin is not stopped during illness, even when not eating, and ketones are checked.

alternative_dispositions.label: Intensive care unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Safe, and more than she needs. She is alert with mild ketoacidosis. Some hospitals send every insulin infusion to intensive care, and in those hospitals this is the right answer.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: The consensus report suggests a regular unit for mild ketoacidosis, so this is defensible where the unit can check a glucose every hour, run intravenous potassium on a monitor and follow a subcutaneous insulin protocol. Many cannot, and her potassium is the reason to ask.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: The consensus report lists an observation unit for mild ketoacidosis, and some departments run a subcutaneous insulin protocol there. A potassium that started at 3.1 and needs intravenous replacement on a monitor makes her a poor fit unless the unit is set up for it.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home
alternative_dispositions.explanation: She is still in ketoacidosis. It takes hours of insulin for the ketones to clear, and she cannot yet keep fluid down. This is the outcome the triage story leads to if nobody checks a sugar.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to another hospital
alternative_dispositions.explanation: This hospital has everything she needs.

correct_diagnosis.label: Diabetic ketoacidosis
correct_diagnosis.explanation:
A glucose of 348, blood ketones of 4.2 mmol/L and a pH of 7.27 with a bicarbonate of 16 in a patient with type 1 diabetes. All three parts of the definition are present. With a pH above 7.25, a bicarbonate of 15 to 18 and a clear head it is mild.

Mild describes the acidosis. It does not describe the risk. Her potassium was low before treatment, and the usual first drug would have made it dangerous.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypokalemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The finding that changed the order of treatment. The receiving team needs to know it was 3.1 on arrival, because insulin will keep pushing it down and it needs checking every two to four hours.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypomagnesemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A low magnesium makes a low potassium harder to correct. Worth naming so it is replaced and rechecked.

additional_diagnoses.label: Viral gastroenteritis
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The trigger. Naming it tells the next team that the search for a cause was made and that no other source was found on examination or in the urine.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypovolemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: She was dry from vomiting, diarrhea and the glucose in her urine. True, and treated with the first bolus.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Viral gastroenteritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She has it, and as the main diagnosis it stops one step short. Gastroenteritis explains the vomiting. It does not explain a glucose of 348, deep breathing or a bicarbonate of 16. This is the diagnosis that sends her home. Name it beside the ketoacidosis as the trigger.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Infectious gastroenteritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The trigger and not the problem that needs a hospital bed. The glucose, the ketones and the gas make the diagnosis.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypokalemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True, and the most dangerous number she has. It is a complication. The diagnosis that explains the admission is the ketoacidosis. Name this beside it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Anion gap metabolic acidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Correct as a description of the gas and the chemistry. With a high glucose and ketones of 4.2 the cause is known, and the handover should say it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypovolemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True and incomplete. Fluid alone left her bicarbonate and anion gap where they were.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: That is a much higher glucose and osmolality with little ketosis, usually in an older patient with type 2 diabetes. Her glucose is 348, her osmolality is normal and her ketones are high.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Ketoacidosis after heavy drinking and poor intake, usually with a normal or low glucose. She drinks little, had none this week, and has type 1 diabetes with a glucose of 348.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute pancreatitis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Worth a thought with vomiting and abdominal pain, and it can trigger ketoacidosis. Her pain is crampy and diffuse, her abdomen is soft and her lipase is normal.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute appendicitis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her appendix was removed when she was fifteen, and her abdomen has no localized tenderness.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hyperemesis gravidarum
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her pregnancy test is negative. It was right to check.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She does not use cannabis, and it does not cause a high glucose with ketones.

debrief_configuration.key_exams_note: Every exam is tagged neutral, so the Physical score reads this list: the deep breathing, the perfusion, the dry mouth, the abdomen and the mental state. Model judgment.
debrief_configuration.intended_path_note: Fluid, the chemistry, potassium, a repeat level, then insulin. A learner who gives insulin first passes through potassium_falling and recovering and reaches the same end.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: Know the potassium before you give insulin. Under 3.5, replace it and hold insulin until it is back above 3.5. Insulin, bicarbonate and fluid all push potassium down.
A vomiting adult who looks dry or is breathing deeply gets a bedside glucose. Ketoacidosis often arrives looking like a stomach bug.
Fluid treats the dehydration and insulin treats the ketoacidosis. When the glucose falls under 250, add dextrose and keep the insulin going until the ketones clear.
Mild describes the pH. It does not describe the risk. The most dangerous number in this patient was not the glucose.
Patients who stop eating often stop their insulin. In type 1 diabetes basal insulin is not stopped during illness, even when not eating, and that teaching is part of the discharge.
The simulator compresses hours into seconds and does not model doses. The order of the steps is the lesson, and the timings are not.
